verses.zh: 约伯回答说：
verses.en: Then Job answered:

verses.zh: 你们要细听我的言语，就算是你们安慰我。
verses.en: “Listen carefully[NOTE:1] to my words;let this be[NOTE:2] the consolation you offer me.[NOTE:3]
notes: In this chapter Job actually answers the ideas of all three of his friends. Here Job finds the flaw in their argument—he can point to wicked people who prosper. But whereas in the last speech, when he looked on his suffering from the perspective of his innocence, he found great faith and hope, in this chapter when he surveys the divine government of the world, he sinks to despair. The speech can be divided into five parts: he appeals for a hearing (2-6), he points out the prosperity of the wicked (7-16), he wonders exactly when the godless suffer (17-22), he shows how death levels everything (23-26), and he reveals how experience contradicts his friends’ argument (27-34).
The intensity of the appeal is again expressed by the imperative followed by the infinitive absolute for emphasis. See note on “listen carefully” in 13:17.
The LXX negates the sentence, “that I may not have this consolation from you.”

verses.zh: 请宽容我，我又要说话；说了以后，任凭你们嗤笑吧！
verses.en: Bear with me[NOTE:1] and I[NOTE:2] will speak,and after I have spoken[NOTE:3] you may mock.[NOTE:4]
notes: The word תַּנְחוּמֹתֵיכֶם (tankhumotekhem) is literally “your consolations,” the suffix being a subjective genitive. The friends had thought they were offering Job consolation (Job 15:11), but the consolation he wants from them is that they listen to him and respond accordingly.
The verb נָשָׂא (nasaʾ) means “to lift up; to raise up,” but in this context it means “to endure; to tolerate” (see Job 7:21).
The conjunction and the independent personal pronoun draw emphatic attention to the subject of the verb: “and I on my part will speak.”
The adverbial clauses are constructed of the preposition “after” and the Piel infinitive construct with the subjective genitive suffix: “my speaking,” or “I speak.”

verses.zh: 我岂是向人诉冤？为何不焦急呢？
verses.en: Is my[NOTE:1] complaint against a man?[NOTE:2] If so,[NOTE:3] why should I not be impatient?[NOTE:4]
notes: The verb is the imperfect of לָעַג (laʿag). The Hiphil has the same basic sense as the Qal, “to mock; to deride.” The imperfect here would be modal, expressing permission. The verb is in the singular, suggesting that Job is addressing Zophar; however, most of the versions put it into the plural. Note the singular in 16:3 between the plural in 16:1 and 16:4.
The addition of the independent pronoun at the beginning of the sentence (“Is it I / against a man / my complaint”) strengthens the pronominal suffix on “complaint” (see GKC 438 §135.f).

The point seems to be that if his complaint were merely against men he might expect sympathy from other men, but no one dares offer him sympathy when his complaint is against God. So he will give free expression to his spirit (H. H. Rowley, Job [NCBC], 147).
On disjunctive interrogatives, see GKC 475 §150.g.

verses.zh: 你们要看着我而惊奇，用手捂口。
verses.en: Look[NOTE:1] at me and be appalled;put your hands over your mouths.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “why should my spirit/breath not be short” (see Num 21:4; Judg 16:16).

The verb פְּנוּ (penu) is from the verb “to turn,” related to the word for “face.” In calling for them to turn toward him, he is calling for them to look at him. But here it may be more in the sense of their attention rather than just a looking at him.

verses.zh: 我每逢思想，心就惊惶，浑身战兢。
verses.en: For, when I think about[NOTE:1] this, I am terrified[NOTE:2] and my body feels a shudder.[NOTE:3]
notes: The idiom is “put a hand over a mouth,” the natural gesture for keeping silent and listening (cf. Job 29:9; 40:4; Mic 7:16).
The verb is זָכַר (zakhar, “to remember”). Here it has the sense of “to keep in memory; to meditate; to think upon.”
The main clause is introduced here by the conjunction, following the adverbial clause of time.

verses.zh: 恶人为何存活，享大寿数，势力强盛呢？
verses.en: “Why do the wicked go on living,[NOTE:1] grow old,[NOTE:2] even increase in power?
notes: Some commentators take “shudder” to be the subject of the verb, “a shudder seizes my body.” But the word is feminine (and see the usage, especially in Job 9:6 and 18:20). It is the subject in Isa 21:4; Ps 55:6; and Ezek 7:18.
A. B. Davidson (Job, 154) clarifies that Job’s question is of a universal scope. In the government of God, why do the wicked exist at all? The verb could be translated “continue to live.”

verses.zh: 他们眼见儿孙，和他们一同坚立。
verses.en: Their children[NOTE:1] are firmly established in their presence,[NOTE:2] their offspring before their eyes.
notes: The verb עָתַק (ʿataq) means “to move; to proceed; to advance.” Here it is “to advance in years” or “to grow old.” This clause could serve as an independent clause, a separate sentence, but it more likely continues the question of the first colon and is parallel to the verb “live.”
Heb “their seed.”

verses.zh: 他们的家宅平安无惧；　神的杖也不加在他们身上。
verses.en: Their houses are safe[NOTE:1] and without fear;[NOTE:2] and no rod of punishment[NOTE:3] from God is upon them.[NOTE:4]
notes: The text uses לִפְנֵיהֶם עִמָּם (lifnehem ʿimmam, “before them, with them”). Many editors think that these were alternative readings, and so omit one or the other. Dhorme moved עִמָּם (ʿimmam) to the second half of the verse and emended it to read עֹמְדִים (ʿomedim, “abide”). Kissane and Gordis changed only the vowels and came up with עַמָּם (ʿammam, “their kinfolk”). But Gordis thinks the presence of both of them in the line is evidence of a conflated reading (p. 229).
The word שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace, safety”) is here a substantive after a plural subject (see GKC 452 §141.c, n. 3).

The form מִפָּחַד (mippakhad) is translated “without fear,” literally “from fear”; the preposition is similar to the alpha privative in Greek. The word “fear, dread” means nothing that causes fear or dread—they are peaceful, secure. See GKC 382 §119.w.
Heb “no rod of God.” The words “punishment from” have been supplied in the translation to make the metaphor understandable for the modern reader by stating the purpose of the rod.

verses.zh: 他们的公牛孳生而不断绝；母牛下犊而不掉胎。
verses.en: Their bulls[NOTE:1] breed[NOTE:2] without fail;[NOTE:3] their cows calve and do not miscarry.
notes: In 9:34 Job was complaining that there was no umpire to remove God’s rod from him, but here he observes no such rod is on the wicked.
Heb “his bull,” but it is meant to signify the bulls of the wicked.
The verb used here means “to impregnate,” and not to be confused with the verb עָבַר (ʿavar, “to pass over”).

verses.zh: 他们打发小孩子出去，多如羊群；他们的儿女踊跃跳舞。
verses.en: They allow their children to run[NOTE:1] like a flock;their little ones dance about.
notes: The use of the verb גָּעַר (gaʿar) in this place is interesting. It means “to rebuke; to abhor; to loathe.” In the causative stem it means “to occasion impurity” or “to reject as loathsome.” The rabbinic interpretation is that it does not emit semen in vain, and so the meaning is it does not fail to breed (see E. Dhorme, Job, 311; R. Gordis, Job, 229).

verses.zh: 他们随着琴鼓歌唱，又因箫声欢喜。
verses.en: They sing[NOTE:1] to the accompaniment of tambourine and harp,and make merry to the sound of the flute.
notes: The verb שָׁלַח (shalakh) means “to send forth,” but in the Piel “to release; to allow to run free.” The picture of children frolicking in the fields and singing and dancing is symbolic of peaceful, prosperous times.

verses.zh: 他们度日诸事亨通，转眼下入阴间。
verses.en: They live out[NOTE:1] their years in prosperityand go down[NOTE:2] to the grave[NOTE:3] in peace.
notes: The verb is simply “they take up [or lift up],” but the understood object is “their voices,” and so it means “they sing.”

The Kethib has “they wear out” but the Qere and the versions have יְכַלּוּ (yekhallu, “bring to an end”). The verb כָּלָה (kalah) means “to finish; to complete,” and here with the object “their days,” it means that they bring their life to a (successful) conclusion. Both readings are acceptable in the context, with very little difference in the overall meaning (which according to Gordis is proof the Qere does not always correct the Kethib).

The MT has יֵחָתּוּ (yekhattu, “they are frightened [or broken]”), taking the verb from חָתַת (khatat, “be terrified”). But most would slightly repoint it to יֵחָתוּ (yekhatu), an Aramaism, “they go down,” from נָחַת (nakhat, “go down”). See Job 17:16.

verses.zh: 他们对　神说：离开我们吧！我们不愿晓得你的道。
verses.en: So they say to God, ‘Turn away from us!We do not want to know your ways.[NOTE:1]
notes: The word רֶגַע (regaʿ) has been interpreted as “in a moment” or “in peace” (on the basis of Arabic rajaʿa, “return to rest”). Gordis thinks this is a case of talhin— both meanings present in the mind of the writer.

verses.zh: 全能者是谁，我们何必事奉他呢？求告他有甚么益处呢？
verses.en: Who is the Almighty, that[NOTE:1] we should serve him?What would we gain if we were to pray[NOTE:2] to him?’[NOTE:3]
notes: Contrast Ps 25:4, which affirms that walking in God’s ways means to obey God’s will—the Torah.
The interrogative clause is followed by ki, similar to Exod 5:2, “Who is Yahweh, that I should obey him?”
The verb פָּגַע (pagaʿ) means “to encounter; to meet,” but also “to meet with request; to intercede; to interpose.” The latter meaning is a derived meaning by usage.

verses.zh: 看哪，他们亨通不在乎自己；恶人所谋定的离我好远。
verses.en: But their prosperity is not their own doing.[NOTE:1] The counsel of the wicked is far from me![NOTE:2]
notes: The verse is not present in the LXX. It may be that it was considered too blasphemous and therefore omitted.

Heb “is not in their hand.”sn The implication of this statement is that their well-being is from God, which is the problem Job is raising in the chapter. A number of commentators make it a question, interpreting it to mean that the wicked enjoy prosperity as if it is their right. Some emend the text to say “his hands”—Gordis reads it, “Indeed, our prosperity is not in his hands.”

verses.zh: 恶人的灯何尝熄灭？患难何尝临到他们呢？　神何尝发怒，向他们分散灾祸呢？
verses.en: “How often[NOTE:1] is the lamp of the wicked extinguished?How often does their[NOTE:2] misfortune come upon them?How often does God apportion pain[NOTE:3] to them[NOTE:4] in his anger?
notes: Even though their life seems so good in contrast to his own plight, Job cannot and will not embrace their principles—“far be from me their counsel.”
The interrogative “How often” occurs only with the first colon; it is supplied for smoother reading in the next two.

The pronominal suffix is objective; it re-enforces the object of the preposition, “upon them.” The verb in the clause is בּוֹא (boʾ) followed by עַל (ʿal), “come upon [or against],” may be interpreted as meaning attack or strike.

חֲבָלִים (khavalim) can mean “ropes” or “cords,” but that would not go with the verb “apportion” in this line. The meaning of “pangs (as in “birth-pangs”) seems to fit best here. The wider meaning would be “physical agony.”

verses.zh: 他们何尝像风前的碎秸，如暴风刮去的糠秕呢？
verses.en: How often[NOTE:1] are they like straw before the windand like chaff swept away[NOTE:2] by a whirlwind?
notes: The phrase “to them” is understood and thus is supplied in the translation for clarification.
To retain the sense that the wicked do not suffer as others, this verse must either be taken as a question or a continuation of the question in v. 17.

verses.zh: 你们说：　神为恶人的儿女积蓄罪孽；我说：不如本人受报，好使他亲自知道。
verses.en: You may say,[NOTE:1] ‘God stores up a man’s[NOTE:2] punishment for his children!’[NOTE:3] Instead let him repay[NOTE:4] the man himself[NOTE:5] so that[NOTE:6] he may be humbled![NOTE:7]
notes: The verb used actually means “rob.” It is appropriate to the image of a whirlwind suddenly taking away the wisp of straw.

These words are supplied. The verse records an idea that Job suspected they might have, namely, that if the wicked die well God will make their children pay for their sins (see Job 5:4; 20:10; as well as Exod 20:5).
The text simply has אוֹנוֹ (ʾono, “his iniquity”), but by usage, “the punishment for the iniquity.”
Heb “his sons.”
The verb שָׁלַם (shalam) in the Piel has the meaning of restoring things to normal, making whole, and so reward, repay (if for sins), or recompense in general.
The text simply has “let him repay [to] him.”
The imperfect verb after the jussive carries the meaning of a purpose clause, and so taken as a final imperfect: “in order that he may be humbled.”

verses.zh: 愿他亲眼看见自己败亡，亲自饮全能者的忿怒。
verses.en: Let his own eyes see his destruction;[NOTE:1] let him drink of the anger of the Almighty.
notes: The common verb יָדַע (yadaʿ) means “to know.” Among homophonous roots DCH includes יָדַע II meaning “be quiet, at rest; be submissive, humbled” (cf. Prov 5:6; Isa 45:4; Jer 14:18; Hos 9:7).

verses.zh: 他的岁月既尽，他还顾他本家吗？
verses.en: For what is his interest[NOTE:1] in his home after his death,[NOTE:2] when the number of his months has been broken off?[NOTE:3]
notes: This word occurs only here. The word כִּיד (kid) was connected to Arabic kaid, “fraud, trickery,” or “warfare.” The word is emended by the commentators to other ideas, such as פִּיד (pid, “[his] calamity”). Dahood and others alter it to “cup”; Wright to “weapons.” A. F. L. Beeston argues for a meaning “condemnation” for the MT form, and so makes no change in the text (Mus 67 [1954]: 315-16). If the connection to Arabic “warfare” is sustained, or if such explanations of the existing MT can be sustained, then the text need not be emended. In any case, the sense of the line is clear.
Heb “his desire.” The meaning is that after he is gone he does not care about what happens to his household (“house” meaning “family” here).
Heb “after him,” but clearly the meaning is “after he is gone.”

verses.zh: 神既审判那在高位的，谁能将知识教训他呢？
verses.en: Can anyone teach[NOTE:1] God knowledge,since[NOTE:2] he judges those that are on high?[NOTE:3]
notes: The rare word חֻצָּצוּ (khutsatsu) is probably a cognate of hassa in Arabic, meaning “to cut off.” There is also an Akkadian word “to cut in two” and “to break.” These fit the context here rather well. The other Hebrew words that are connected to the root חָצַץ (khatsats) do not offer any help.
The imperfect verb in this question should be given the modal nuance of potential imperfect. The question is rhetorical—it is affirming that no one can teach God.
The clause begins with the disjunctive vav (ו) and the pronoun, “and he.” This is to be subordinated as a circumstantial clause. See GKC 456 §142.d.

verses.zh: 有人至死身体强壮，尽得平靖安逸；
verses.en: “One man dies in his full vigor,[NOTE:1] completely secure and prosperous,
notes: The Hebrew has רָמִים (ramim), a plural masculine participle of רוּם (rum, “to be high; to be exalted”). This is probably a reference to the angels. But M. Dahood restores an older interpretation that it refers to “the Most High” (“Some Northwest Semitic words in Job,”Bib 38 [1957]: 316-17). He would take the word as a singular form with an enclitic mem (ם). He reads the verse, “will he judge the Most High?”

verses.zh: 他的奶桶充满，他的骨髓滋润。
verses.en: his body[NOTE:1] well nourished,[NOTE:2] and the marrow of his bones moist.[NOTE:3]
notes: The line has “in the bone of his perfection.” The word עֶצֶם (ʾetsem), which means “bone,” is used pronominally to express “the same, very”; here it is “in the very fullness of his strength” (see GKC 449 §139.g). The abstract תֹּם (tom) is used here in the sense of physical perfection and strengths.

The verb עָטַן (ʿatan) has the precise meaning of “press olives.” But because here it says “full of milk,” the derived meaning for the noun has been made to mean “breasts” or “pails” (although in later Hebrew this word occurs—but with olives, not with milk). Dhorme takes it to refer to “his sides,” and repoints the word for “milk” (חָלָב, khalav) to get “fat” (חֶלֶב, khelev)—“his sides are full of fat,” a rendering followed by NASB. However, this weakens the parallelism.
This interpretation, adopted by several commentaries and modern translations (cf. NAB, NIV), is a general rendering to capture the sense of the line.

verses.zh: 有人至死心中痛苦，终身未尝福乐的滋味；
verses.en: And another man[NOTE:1] dies in bitterness of soul,[NOTE:2] never having tasted[NOTE:3] anything good.
notes: The verb שָׁקָה (shaqah) means “to water” and here “to be watered thoroughly.” The picture in the line is that of health and vigor.
The expression “this (v. 23)…and this” (v. 25) means “one…the other.”

The text literally has “and this [man] dies in soul of bitterness.” Some simply reverse it and translate “in the bitterness of soul.” The genitive “bitterness” may be an attribute adjective, “with a bitter soul.”

verses.zh: 他们一样躺卧在尘土中，都被虫子遮盖。
verses.en: Together they lie down in the dust,and worms cover over them both.

verses.zh: 我知道你们的意思，并诬害我的计谋。
verses.en: “Yes, I know what you are thinking,[NOTE:1] the schemes[NOTE:2] by which you would wrong me.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “eaten what is good.” It means he died without having enjoyed the good life.

The word is “your thoughts.” The word for “thoughts” (from חָצַב [khatsav, “to think; to reckon; to plan”]) has more to do with their intent than their general thoughts. He knows that when they talked about the fate of the wicked they really were talking about him.
For the meaning of this word, and its root זָמַם (zamam), see Job 17:11. It usually means the “plans” or “schemes” that are concocted against someone.

verses.zh: 你们说：霸者的房屋在哪里？恶人住过的帐棚在哪里？
verses.en: For you say, ‘Where now is the nobleman’s house,[NOTE:1] and where are the tents in which the wicked lived?’[NOTE:2]
notes: E. Dhorme (Job, 321) distinguishes the verb חָמַס (khamas) from the noun for “violence.” He proposes a meaning of “think, imagine”: “and the ideas you imagined about me.”
The question implies the answer will be “vanished” or “gone.”

verses.zh: 你们岂没有询问过路的人吗？不知道他们所引的证据吗？
verses.en: Have you never questioned those who travel the roads?Do you not recognize their accounts[NOTE:1]—
notes: Heb “And where is the tent, the dwellings of the wicked.” The word “dwellings of the wicked” is in apposition to “tent.” A relative pronoun must be supplied in the translation.

verses.zh: 就是恶人在祸患的日子得存留，在发怒的日子得逃脱。
verses.en: that the evil man is sparedfrom the day of his misfortune,that he is delivered[NOTE:1] from the day of God’s wrath?
notes: The LXX reads, “Ask those who go by the way, and do not disown their signs.”tn The idea is that the merchants who travel widely will talk about what they have seen and heard. These travelers give a different account of the wicked; they tell how he is spared. E. Dhorme (Job, 322) interprets “signs” concretely: “Their custom was to write their names and their thoughts somewhere at the main cross-roads. The main roads of Sinai are dotted with these scribblings made by such passers of a day.”

verses.zh: 他所行的，有谁当面给他说明？他所做的，有谁报应他呢？
verses.en: No one denounces his conduct to his face;no one repays him for what[NOTE:1] he has done.[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb means “to be led forth.” To be “led forth in the day of trouble” means to be delivered.
The expression “and he has done” is taken here to mean “what he has done.”

verses.zh: 然而他要被抬到茔地；并有人看守坟墓。
verses.en: And when he is carried to the tombsand watch is kept[NOTE:1] over the funeral mound,[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Who declares his way to his face? // Who repays him for what he has done?” These rhetorical questions, which expect a negative answer (“No one!”) have been translated as indicative statements to bring out their force clearly.
The verb says “he will watch.” The subject is unspecified, so the translation is passive.

verses.zh: 他要以谷中的土块为甘甜；在他以先去的无数，在他以后去的更多。
verses.en: the clods of the torrent valley[NOTE:1] are sweet to him;behind him everybody follows in procession,and before him goes a countless throng.
notes: The Hebrew word refers to the tumulus, the burial mound that is erected on the spot where the person is buried.

verses.zh: 你们对答的话中既都错谬，怎么徒然安慰我呢？
verses.en: So how can you console me with your futile words?Nothing is left of your answers but deception!”[NOTE:1]
notes: The clods are those that are used to make a mound over the body. And, for a burial in the valley, see Deut 34:6. The verse here sees him as participating in his funeral and enjoying it. Nothing seems to go wrong with the wicked.
